analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal watchdog over banks, lenders, and debt collectors.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a vote; the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would repeal the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, which created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) — the agency that supervises banks and lenders and takes enforcement action over practices like junk fees, abusive debt collection, and misleading mortgage and credit card terms. Repealing it would erase the bureau and put consumer protection rules back under the weaker, scattered system that existed before 2010. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies would gain: they would no longer face a single federal agency dedicated to supervising their consumer practices and fining them for abuses.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, the law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
Restores or revives the pre-2010 legal framework, un-doing the changes that Act made to federal consumer financial law.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers with mortgages, credit cards, student loans, bank accounts, and debts would lose the agency that polices hidden fees, discriminatory lending, and abusive collection practices, and would have to rely on a patchwork of weaker regulators.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would leave no dedicated consumer watchdog: the CFPB returns billions to consumers through enforcement and supervises lenders that other regulators historically overlooked, and the bill offers no replacement mechanism.

The strongest good-faith argument for repeal is that the bureau concentrates power in a single director whose funding comes outside the normal congressional appropriations process, which supporters of the bill view as unaccountable. That is a structural complaint, not a proposal for how consumer protection rules would be enforced without the bureau.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's entire effect is subtraction: it removes a consumer protection agency and restores the pre-2010 status quo, without replacing any of its functions. Whatever its structural objections, the bill gave no answer to who would police abusive lending and debt collection afterward — so the practical cost would fall on consumers, and the practical benefit on the regulated companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Byron Donalds introduced the bill on January 14, 2022, joined by four Republican cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee at the end of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers kept the CFPB, its supervision of lenders, and its enforcement of refund and penalty rulings, because the bill never advanced. The banks and lenders that would have benefited from repeal gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Byron Donalds
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Consumer Financial Protection Act and abolish the CFPB.

for.name: Reps. Ted Budd, Alex Mooney, and Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill; no other members signed on.

against.name: Chair Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it remained in referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat with the Democratic-controlled Financial Services Committee without action.

industries.industry: Banks, consumer lenders, and credit card issuers
industries.note: Repeal would end CFPB supervision and enforcement against hidden fees, discriminatory lending, and misleading card terms — costs these firms currently bear. Their gain would come at consumers' expense.

industries.industry: Payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: These are among the industries the CFPB most frequently polices; repeal would remove the agency that brings those cases.
